plague-of-justinian.summary: Reached Constantinople in 541 and returned in waves for two centuries, crippling Justinian's attempt to reunite the Roman world.
plague-of-justinian.note: The first documented pandemic of Yersinia pestis, confirmed by DNA recovered from sixth-century graves. Death tolls are heavily disputed; older estimates of half the Mediterranean population are now widely doubted.

gokturk-khaganate.summary: The first state to call itself Türk, stretching from Manchuria to the Black Sea, and the source of the Orkhon inscriptions — the earliest surviving texts in any Turkic language.

muhammad.summary: Founder of Islam, whose revelations became the Quran and whose community at Medina grew into a polity that unified the Arabian peninsula.

sui-dynasty.summary: Reunified China after three centuries of division and built the Grand Canal, exhausting itself in the process and lasting barely a generation.

brahmagupta.summary: Gave the first known rules for arithmetic with zero and negative numbers, treating debt and nothingness as numbers in their own right.

wari.summary: Built the administrative and road systems across the Andes that the Inca would later inherit and extend.

grand-canal.summary: Nearly 1,800 km linking the Yangtze rice country to the northern capitals, the longest artificial waterway ever built and still in use.

tang-dynasty.summary: A cosmopolitan high point of Chinese poetry, Buddhism and long-distance trade, centred on Chang'an, then the largest city on Earth.
tang-dynasty.significance: Chang'an was probably the largest city on Earth, with resident Persian, Sogdian, Japanese and Korean communities. Cosmopolitanism is not a modern invention.

quran-codified.summary: Roughly two decades after Muhammad's death, a standard written version was established and variant copies withdrawn — the shortest gap between a founder and a fixed text of any major tradition.
quran-codified.significance: About two decades - the shortest gap between a founder and a fixed text of any major tradition, and the reason its textual history is argued on different grounds from the others.
quran-codified.note: Islamic doctrine holds the Quran to be the uncreated word of God, recited by Muhammad and memorised and written by companions during his lifetime; the caliph Uthman's work was standardisation of an existing text, not composition. Manuscript finds at Sana'a are broadly consistent with an early fixed text.

texts.title: Islamic texts at the Internet Sacred Text Archive

srivijaya.summary: A Buddhist maritime power controlling the Malacca and Sunda straits, and a centre of Buddhist learning that Chinese pilgrims stopped at on their way to India.

trans-saharan-trade.summary: Enslaved people were moved north across the desert alongside gold and salt for more than a millennium — the longest-running of the trades in African people, and the least documented.
trans-saharan-trade.note: Estimates of around nine million people trafficked over thirteen centuries are extrapolations from fragmentary records, and are disputed.

woodblock-printing.summary: Printing from carved blocks produced the world's earliest dated printed book in 868, some six centuries before Gutenberg.
woodblock-printing.significance: It produced the world's earliest dated printed book in 868, six centuries before Gutenberg, and stayed better suited than movable type to a script of tens of thousands of characters.
woodblock-printing.note: The bar ends where movable type takes over in Europe; block printing remained in use across East Asia long after.

image.credit: The colophon, at the inner end, reads: Reverently [caused to be] made for universal free distribution by Wang Jie on behalf of his two parents on the 13th of the 4th moon of the 9th year of Xiantong [i.e. 11th May, CE 868 ].

bhavabhuti.summary: The dramatist most often named in the same breath as Kalidasa, and the one who took Sanskrit drama towards grief and away from charm.

adi-shankara.summary: Systematised Advaita Vedanta, arguing that the self and ultimate reality are not two things, and debated his way across the subcontinent.
adi-shankara.significance: He argued his way across the subcontinent and reorganised Hindu thought around non-dualism. Ramanuja's reply, a century later, opened devotion to those outside the upper castes.
adi-shankara.note: Traditional dates give 788-820; many historians prefer the early eighth century. Both are inferences from later hagiography.

islamic-calligraphy.summary: With figural images discouraged in religious settings, Islamic art put its inventive weight into the written word and into geometry — producing scripts treated as fine art and tiling patterns that mathematicians are still writing papers about.

kanem-bornu.summary: One of the longest-lived states in African history, controlling the central Saharan trade routes around Lake Chad for roughly a millennium.

li-bai.summary: The Tang poet of wine, moonlight and the road, who wrote as though the poem had cost him nothing, and whose reputation in China has never since been out of the first rank.

du-fu.summary: Li Bai's contemporary and opposite — a poet of war, hunger and exile whose craft was so exact that later critics called him simply the poet-historian.

uyghur-khaganate.summary: Steppe empire that adopted Manichaeism as a state religion and propped up the Tang dynasty after the An Lushan rebellion, at a price.

an-lushan-rebellion.summary: A revolt that broke the Tang at its height, and by the census numbers is sometimes counted among the deadliest conflicts in history.
an-lushan-rebellion.note: Census figures show a fall of some 36 million, but much of that is collapse of the registration system rather than deaths. The rebellion was nonetheless catastrophic.

al-khwarizmi.summary: Set out systematic methods for solving equations, giving algebra its name, and carried Indian decimal numerals into the wider world.

borobudur.summary: The largest Buddhist monument in the world, a stepped stone mandala in central Java, abandoned within a century and a half and overgrown for most of a millennium.

heian-period.summary: An aristocratic court culture that produced The Tale of Genji, often called the first novel, written by a noblewoman at the turn of the eleventh century.

indian-ocean-slave-trade.summary: Enslaved East Africans were carried to Arabia, Persia and India over a comparably long period, with Zanzibar as the principal market in the nineteenth century.

maya-collapse.summary: Within roughly a century the great lowland cities were given up and monument-carving stopped.
maya-collapse.note: Drought, warfare, soil exhaustion and political fragmentation are all argued for, probably in combination. The Maya themselves did not disappear and number in the millions today; it was the southern city-states that were abandoned.

swahili-coast.summary: Kilwa, Mombasa, Zanzibar and their neighbours traded gold, ivory and enslaved people across the Indian Ocean as far as China, producing a Bantu-Arabic language and an urban culture of stone towns.

khmer-empire.summary: Ruled mainland Southeast Asia from Angkor, a hydraulic city whose reservoirs and canals supported a population larger than any pre-industrial urban centre in Europe.

samanid-empire.summary: Presided over a Persian literary and scientific revival centred on Bukhara, whose library and patronage produced Avicenna and Ferdowsi's Shahnameh.

karakhanid-khanate.summary: The first Turkic dynasty to adopt Islam, which set the religious course of Central Asia for the next thousand years.

hadith-collections.summary: The reports of Muhammad's sayings and conduct were sifted and compiled roughly two centuries after his death, by compilers who developed an entire science of chain-of-transmission criticism to do it.

chola-empire.summary: A Tamil maritime empire that projected power to Sri Lanka, the Maldives and Srivijaya, and built the Brihadisvara temple at Thanjavur.
chola-empire.significance: A rare Indian sea power. Its raids on Srivijaya show the subcontinent projecting force across the Bay of Bengal, which is not how Indian history is usually told.

chaco-canyon.summary: Ancestral Puebloan great houses of several hundred rooms, aligned to solar and lunar cycles and linked by engineered roads running straight across the desert for tens of kilometres.

gunpowder.summary: Found by alchemists looking for an elixir of immortality, and in use in weapons within two centuries. It ended the long military advantage of the steppe cavalry and, with it, an age.
gunpowder.significance: It ended the thousand-year military advantage of steppe cavalry, which closes the Central Asia lane as a source of world-conquering empires.
gunpowder.note: From the first formulae to firearms reshaping warfare on three continents.

al-farabi.summary: Known as the Second Teacher after Aristotle, he transmitted Greek logic and political philosophy into Arabic and influenced everyone who followed him in that tradition.

chimu.summary: Ruled the Peruvian coast from Chan Chan, the largest adobe city ever built, until the Inca cut its water supply and absorbed it.

chinese-landscape-painting.summary: Song painters treated landscape not as a setting for figures but as the subject itself, with human figures deliberately tiny — a scale of attention European painting did not attempt for another six hundred years.

goryeo-dynasty.summary: Gave Korea its English name, produced celadon ceramics of exceptional quality, and printed with metal movable type decades before Gutenberg.

ferdowsi.summary: Who spent some thirty years writing the Shahnameh, fifty thousand couplets of Persian legend and history, and is widely credited with carrying the Persian language through the centuries after the Arab conquest.

tui-tonga-empire.summary: A maritime chiefdom whose influence reached Fiji and Samoa, with monumental stone tombs and a hereditary line lasting nearly a millennium.

song-dynasty.summary: A commercial and technological high point — paper money, movable type, the mariner's compass, gunpowder weapons and blast furnaces — all under a state run by examination-selected scholars rather than warriors.
song-dynasty.significance: Paper money, movable type, the compass and gunpowder weapons all in one dynasty. Europe would acquire these over the following four centuries and call the result a revolution.

ibn-al-haytham.summary: Showed that vision works by light entering the eye and insisted claims be tested by experiment, an early statement of scientific method.

al-biruni.summary: Polymath from Khwarazm who measured the Earth's radius from a mountain observation, and wrote a study of India notable for trying to describe a foreign culture on its own terms.

avicenna.summary: Born near Bukhara, he wrote a medical encyclopaedia used as a standard text in Europe for six centuries and a philosophical system that shaped both Islamic and scholastic thought.

kula-ring.summary: A ceremonial exchange of shell valuables circulating in opposite directions between Melanesian islands, studied in the 1910s and foundational to the anthropology of gift economies.

norse-vinland.summary: Norse from Greenland built a small settlement in Newfoundland, stayed briefly, and left — nearly five centuries before Columbus, with no lasting consequence.
norse-vinland.note: Tree-ring dating of wood at L'Anse aux Meadows fixes occupation to exactly 1021 CE, the earliest precisely dated European presence in the Americas.

settlement-of-hawaii.summary: Voyagers from the Marquesas or Society Islands crossed more than three thousand kilometres of open ocean to reach the most isolated archipelago on Earth.
settlement-of-hawaii.note: Radiocarbon re-dating has pulled the arrival several centuries later than mid-twentieth-century estimates.

variolation.summary: Deliberate infection with material from a mild smallpox case to produce immunity — risky, but the first effective control of an epidemic disease, and the practice vaccination replaced.
variolation.note: Practised in China, India, the Ottoman empire and West Africa well before it reached Europe; the earliest dates are not securely established.
